title: NORDIS assesses threats to the Danish information environment
content:
NORDIS partner TjekDet has published a comprehensive written threat assessment of misinformation, disinformation and other developments that may affect the Danish information environment.

Denmark continues to have a strong information environment. But the ways in which misinformation emerges, spreads and affects us are changing constantly and rapidly.

This is the starting point for the Threat Assessment 2026, which brings together the NORDIS and TjekDet’s editorial team’s assessment of the most significant threats to the Danish information environment.

One of the report’s overall conclusions is that Denmark continues to have a fundamentally robust information environment, but also that the threat landscape has become far more complex than it was just five or six years ago.

title: October 14, 2026: NORDIS partners gather for closing conference
content:
On 14 October 2026, the NORDIS consortium meets at Faktisk.no in Oslo for the NORDIS 2 Closing Conference, bringing together partners from across the Nordic region to reflect on the project’s achievements, share key lessons and discuss future collaboration.

Throughout the day, partners will present their main contributions and takeaways from the second phase of NORDIS, covering fact-checking, research, media literacy and technological innovation.

The conference will also look ahead to the next round of the Nordic Hub, with a dedicated session on building a Nordic “Network of Networks” to strengthen cooperation and information integrity across the region.

title: The world has a new answer to disinformation. But is it asking the right questions?
content:
From the UN to the EU, “information integrity” has become a guiding principle for protecting democracy and strengthening the information environment. A new NORDIS policy brief examines what the concept promises, what it overlooks – and why the same solutions may not work everywhere.

The fight against disinformation has a new vocabulary. Governments and international organisations increasingly speak of information integrity – a concept intended to address not only false and misleading information, but also the wider conditions that shape how people access, share and trust information.

In just a few years, the term has gained prominence in policy frameworks developed by the United Nations, the OECD, the European Union and the Council of Europe.

But what does information integrity actually mean? And can a concept broad enough to encompass journalism, artificial intelligence, elections, media literacy and public trust provide meaningful solutions to the challenges facing different societies?

These are among the questions explored in a new NORDIS policy brief, Interrogating Information Integrity: What the Concept Includes, What It Misses, and What Comes Next.
